analysis.one_liner: Lets the government negotiate lower prescription drug prices for Medicare beneficiaries.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require drug makers that sell covered outpatient drugs to the federal government to supply pharmacies and Medicare providers at prices negotiated by the Secretary of Health and Human Services, working with the Defense and Veterans Affairs departments. A manufacturer that refused could be barred from federal contracts for a period of time. It also would create an ombudsman to stop pharmacies from marking up prices above the negotiated level, especially in rural areas with little competition.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who pay out of pocket for many prescription drugs, would get drugs at federally negotiated prices. Pharmacies and Medicare providers would buy at those negotiated prices, and an ombudsman would police resellers who inflate prices above them.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each participating manufacturer to make covered outpatient drugs available to any pharmacy and to Medicare providers, physicians, practitioners, and suppliers at a price negotiated by the Secretary of Health and Human Services with the Defense and Veterans Affairs secretaries.
Lets the government bar from federal contracting, for a period of time, any drug maker that does not comply with the negotiated prices.

Directs the Secretary to set up a dispute-resolution mechanism, such as an ombudsman, to protect beneficiaries from resellers artificially inflating prices in low-competition areas like rural communities and from price collusion elsewhere.
Requires annual reports to Congress on whether the law is reducing drug prices for Medicare beneficiaries, with recommendations for further reductions.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would sell their Medicare-volume drugs at lower negotiated prices, cutting their revenue on those sales. Supporters of higher drug prices typically argue such negotiations reduce the revenue available for research on new drugs.

drawbacks.text: The main enforcement tool is debarment from federal contracting. If the government actually barred a major drug maker from contracts, it could cut off Medicare beneficiaries' access to that company's drugs, a risk the bill does not address.

The negotiation duty applies only to 'participating manufacturers' — those that enter contracts with the United States to sell covered drugs — so manufacturers outside that arrangement would not be bound by it.

The bill directs negotiators to account for promoting breakthrough drugs but sets no standard for how much weight to give drug makers' research concerns, leaving real trade-offs between lower prices today and innovation incentives unresolved.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries facing high out-of-pocket drug costs, the benefit of federally negotiated prices would be large and direct. The main costs fall on drug manufacturers, whose Medicare sales would earn less, with some risk that slower revenue growth affects research on new drugs. The bill's enforcement design is crude — threatening to cut off a noncompliant manufacturer's entire federal business could backfire by removing a needed drug from the market — and the bill does nothing for people under 65.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees, passed to their health subcommittees within two weeks, and never came up for a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John B. Larson (D-CT) introduced the Medicare Prescription Drug Price Negotiation Act on October 15, 2003, to provide prescription drugs at reduced prices to Medicare beneficiaries.
The bill had 19 cosponsors: 18 Democrats and 1 Republican.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on October 15, 2003.

On October 20 and October 27, 2003, it was referred to the health subcommittees of those committees; the record shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: the bill died without a vote, and a month after it was introduced Congress passed the Medicare Modernization Act, which included a provision barring the government from interfering with drug price negotiations between manufacturers and pharmacies.

for.name: Rep. John B. Larson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 15, 2003 and gave introductory remarks on it.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on October 15, 2003 and its Health Subcommittee on October 20, 2003, and took no further recorded action.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee and its Health Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on October 15, 2003 and its Health Subcommittee on October 27, 2003, and took no further recorded action.

against.name: House Republican leadership (108th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Chose not to bring government drug price negotiation to the floor; in November 2003 the House passed the Medicare Modernization Act instead, which prohibited the government from negotiating or interfering with drug prices negotiated between manufacturers and pharmacies.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and 18 of 19 cosponsors were Democrats, with 1 Republican; the bill never reached a floor vote, and the drug price fight of that Congress split along party lines, with the Republican-led House passing a Medicare drug bill that barred government negotiation.

industries.note: The bill would force manufacturers to sell their Medicare volume at prices negotiated by the government, backed by federal contract debarment. Their interest in blocking it ran against beneficiaries' interest in cheaper drugs.

They would buy drugs at negotiated prices, but the ombudsman provision targets resellers who mark prices up above the negotiated level or collude on pricing, so their pricing freedom would be curtailed while their purchase costs fell.
